Maximus the Confessor
măk´sĭ-mŭs thē kun-fĕs´ẽr
n. (Maximus the Confessor, c. 580–662, monk and theologian, chief opponent of Monothelitism, mutilated and exiled for refusing the imperial compromise on the two wills of Christ)
Latin Maximus, greatest; the title Confessor is given in the East to one who suffered for the faith without being put to death.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Maximus the Confessor stood almost alone against an emperor, a patriarch and a pope. The seventh-century court, hoping to win back the Monophysite provinces, proposed that Christ has two natures but one will — Monothelitism — and published it as imperial doctrine. Maximus saw that this emptied Chalcedon: a nature without a will is not a complete nature, and if Christ has no human will then He has no complete humanity, and the obedience by which we are saved was never rendered as man. His proof text is Gethsemane. “Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done” (Luk 22:42) names two wills in one speaker, the human submitting to the divine. Joh 6:38 says the same: “I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me.” Heb 4:15 requires a real human nature tempted in all points. For this Maximus was tried, his tongue cut out and his right hand struck off so that he could neither speak nor write the faith, and he was sent to die in Lazica. The Third Council of Constantinople vindicated him in 681, nineteen years after his death.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the will as that faculty of the mind by which we determine either to do or forbear an action; the faculty which is exercised in deciding.

expand to see more

WILL, n. That faculty or endowment of the soul by which it determines either to do or forbear an action.

2. Choice; determination.

That which is strongly desired or intended; purpose; design.

Key Scripture

Luk 22:42 — "Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done."

Joh 6:38 — "For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me."

Mat 26:39 — "And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt."

Heb 4:15 — "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin."

Modern Corruption

Monothelitism was proposed as a reasonable compromise to heal a schism, which is how the church learns that a compromise on Christ heals nothing.

expand to see more

The imperial doctrine was not a wicked invention; it was a peace plan. The eastern provinces were lost to Monophysitism and the empire needed them, and one will seemed a small price. Maximus answered that it was not a small price but the whole price, because a Christ who lacks a human will lacks a human nature, and the active obedience of a true man is precisely what the gospel requires. The lesson outlasts the controversy: every generation is offered doctrinal concession as the cost of unity, and Gal 2:5 is the apostolic reply — “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.”

A second caution concerns the use made of Maximus today. He is the favourite father of modern Eastern Orthodoxy and is quarried for a scheme of deification in which the creature is drawn up into the divine energies, and for a cosmic reading of salvation that goes well beyond anything Scripture states. Honour his Christology, which is Chalcedon defended at the cost of his tongue and his hand, and decline his speculative anthropology. The believer is united to Christ, adopted, justified and sanctified, and shall be glorified; he does not become what God is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek thelema (G2307), will, that which is willed; thelo (G2309), to will; sumpatheo (G4834), to be touched with feeling.

Greek thelema (G2307) — will, determination; John 6:38.

Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, to be willing; Luke 22:42, Matthew 26:39.

Greek boulomai (G1014) — to purpose, to be minded; Luke 22:42.

Greek sumpatheo (G4834) — to be touched with the feeling of; Hebrews 4:15.

Greek physis (G5449) — nature, that which a thing is.

Usage

"“not my will, but thine, be done” (Luk 22:42) — two wills in one speaker."

"“not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me” (Joh 6:38) — the human will submitting."

"“was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” (Heb 4:15) — a complete humanity required."
